extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in literary/social sketches of gambling and 19th-century travel writing
extracted.subtask_description: Writing vivid social and character sketches of gambling scenes and gamblers, mixing anecdote, description of games, national character, and moral commentary. Focuses on immersive detail, illustrative stories, and contextual/factual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete anecdotes to illustrate types and extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ specific, memorable anecdotes (e.g., the Russian officer who pre-paid his board, the Italian adventurer who alternately stripped the bank and was reduced to a single louis, the emigrant with a basket of tarts who loses all) to show the habits, fortunes, and ruins of gamblers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes should show pattern and consequence (winning and ruin, repeated returns to play). Avoid abstract moralizing unsupported by concrete examples. Vivid, singular stories give emotional force and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich sensory and procedural description of the gaming place
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the layout, objects, sounds, and rituals of the gaming-rooms: 'rooms are well distributed; the saloons handsome', 'not a sound was heard but the rattle of the heaped-up money', piles of coins, cards stripped and shuffled, the croupier's formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tactile/aural/visual details (coins, rouleaux, shuffled cards, verbal formulas) and procedural steps (how games begin, when cards are re-made) to immerse readers. Avoid vague, generic depictions that omit the game's mechanics and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the mechanics of the games encountered
rubrics_metrics.description: Give readers a concise account of how particular games operate (e.g., Trente et Quarante: unpacking the box, arranging rouleaux, packs stripped and shuffled, croupier signals; Roulette: dropping the ball into numbered niches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plainly explain crucial steps or rituals so non-expert readers can follow the scene and stakes. Do not omit mechanics if they are central to dramatic tension or to understanding wins and losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray social composition and class contrasts in the rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Record who frequents the gaming-houses (elite ladies, middle and lower-middle classes, courtesans, diplomats, veterans, street-boys) and how their dress, behaviour, and relative respectability differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts (who is present, who is absent, how they behave) to illuminate social meaning. Provide numberable or named examples where possible. Avoid flattening all participants into a single stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate national or character types through their reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate characteristic reactions to wins and losses with national or personal types: 'Englishmen ... surly, brooding self-reproach'; 'Frenchmen give vent ... by abusing the game'; 'Italians endeavour to conceal discomfiture under gaiety'; 'Russians betray no emotion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small behavioral details (gesture, speech, smoking rate) to signal character or nationality. Avoid caricature that lacks nuance; when invoking national types, anchor observations in scene-specific detail or repeated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use named biographical sketches to humanize the enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch prominent individual figures (e.g., Pat Hern, John Morrissey, Countess C----o) with backstory, mannerisms, and habits to illustrate wider patterns in gambling culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short biographical vignette grounds abstract claims about the trade and its operators. Include specific habits, appearances, and reputed fortunes. Avoid relying solely on rumor—balance anecdote with observable traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate moral and social critique with documentary/contextual material
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine moral commentary ('gambling is a leprosy', 'disgrace of the Rouge et Noir') with newspaper extracts, legislative announcements, and reported profits/indemnities to support judgments and show public response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix opinion with evidence (editorial extracts, bills, statistics) to make social critique persuasive. Beware of one-sided invective without context; include both personal observation and institutional facts where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground narrative with quantitative facts and institutional detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite figures and institutional facts (annual profits to bankers, numbers of Faro banks and policy offices, proposed legal suppression dates) to convey scale and social impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliable-seeming numbers and institutional references to situate anecdotes in a broader factual frame. Clarify sources when possible. Avoid throwing in dubious statistics without attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct speech, formulae, and foreign phrases for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate the language of the place and the game (e.g., the croupier's phrases 'Faites le jeu!', 'Le jeu est fait, rien ne va plus', players' exclamations) to reproduce atmosphere and realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and authentic phrases heighten immediacy. Provide translations or context if readers may not know the language. Overuse of untranslated foreignisms can alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the cyclical and compulsive nature of gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the recurring patterns of play and ruin: repeated returns to the table after losses, moral resolutions quickly abandoned, the alternation of great wins and total ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace sequences over time (one night, the following day, repeated nights) to illustrate addiction's dynamics. Avoid treating single wins or losses as isolated moral lessons; show pattern and compulsion instead.
